etymology: Anglo-Saxon compound sum (some) + thing — an unspecified thing, a matter left deliberately unnamed.
biblical_def:
Something hath befallen him, he is not clean; surely he is not clean. And commanded that something should be given her to eat. For if a man think himself to be something, when he is nothing, he deceiveth himself.

Scripture's something is never idle vagueness; it is precision withheld for a purpose. Jonathan's father supposes something hath befallen David because the plain explanation (open rebellion against the king's table) cannot yet be spoken aloud. The Lord Jesus, having just raised a dead girl, immediately turns to the ordinary: commanded that something should be given her to eat — the miracle does not excuse the household from feeding the child. Paul's usage in Galatians is the most searching of all: the man who thinks himself to be something is the very man who is nothing, and the self-inflation is itself the deception. In every case something marks a gap between what is seen and what is real, and the reader is meant to feel the gap.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): an indeterminate or unknown thing; a portion, quantity, or degree of a thing not specifically named.
webster_full: SOMETHING, n. An indeterminate or unknown event, thing, or portion.
In a less proper sense, a substance or being, indeterminately.
In some degree; a little; as, the report is something incorrect.
Used substantively for a person or thing of consequence, as in 1 Corinthians and Galatians usage.
Distinguished from nothing as substance from vacancy — the very contrast Paul exploits in Gal. 6:3.
scriptures: Nevertheless Saul spake not any thing that day: for he thought, Something hath befallen him, he is not clean; surely he is not clean.
Mar 5:43
And he charged them straitly that no man should know it; and commanded that something should be given her to eat.
Laying wait for him, and seeking to catch something out of his mouth, that they might accuse him.
Gal 6:3
For if a man think himself to be something, when he is nothing, he deceiveth himself.
corruption_summary: Therapeutic self-esteem culture inverts Galatians 6:3 exactly: it insists every man affirm himself to be something as the starting point of health, precisely the posture Paul calls self-deception.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern gospel of self-worth teaches that the cure for despair is to declare yourself something — valuable, worthy, enough — apart from any reference to God. Paul says the opposite: the man convinced of his own something-ness, apart from Christ, is nothing, and thinking otherwise is the deception, not the cure for it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond the self-esteem inversion named above. The principle to recover is Paul's own remedy in the same passage: let every man prove his own work, and boast in Christ alone, not in an unexamined sense of being something.
roots_summary: No single Hebrew or Greek term underlies something; translators supplied it for indefinite constructions, most pointedly Paul's ti (τι), a something or anything, in Gal. 6:3.
roots_lines: Saul's something names a suspicion he will not yet voice outright.
Christ's something after the miracle is ordinary bread, not further wonder.
Paul's something in Galatians is the self-estimate that produces self-deceit.
The Greek ti behind Paul's usage carries the same deliberate vagueness the English preserves.
In every case, something is a placeholder Scripture uses precisely, never carelessly.
usage: Something hath befallen him — Saul's guarded suspicion, not yet named.
Something should be given her to eat — the miracle does not cancel the ordinary means.
To think himself to be something, when he is nothing — Paul's diagnosis of self-deceit.

etymology: Middle English onlesse, from on + lesse (less) — on a lesser condition than; except that.
biblical_def:
Unless he wash his flesh with water. I had fainted, unless I had believed to see the goodness of the LORD in the land of the living. Unless the LORD had been my help, my soul had almost dwelt in silence.

Unless is the conjunction of the single condition on which everything else turns. Leviticus makes it ceremonial: the unclean priest may not eat the holy things unless he first washes, no partial compliance permitted. The Psalter turns it existential and then theological: David's very sanity hung by the thread of unless I had believed, and in Psalm 94 the thread is named outright — unless the LORD had been my help. Paul closes the pattern in 1 Corinthians 15:2, where the gospel itself is held fast unless ye have believed in vain, a warning that saving faith must be a persevering faith, not a momentary assent. Scripture's unless never softens a demand; it isolates the one thing without which nothing else holds.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a conjunctive particle denoting exception; if not; except; supposing that not.
webster_full: UNLESS, conj. If not; supposing that not; except.
It denotes a condition or exception, restraining a preceding proposition.
As, I will not go unless you go with me; that is, if you do not go.
Used in Scripture to isolate a single necessary condition on which a stated outcome depends.
Distinguished from except in that unless more often introduces a hypothetical negative supposition.
scriptures: Lev 22:6
The soul which hath touched any such shall be unclean until even, and shall not eat of the holy things, unless he wash his flesh with water.
I had fainted, unless I had believed to see the goodness of the LORD in the land of the living.
Unless the LORD had been my help, my soul had almost dwelt in silence.
By which also ye are saved, if ye keep in memory what I preached unto you, unless ye have believed in vain.
corruption_summary: Cheap-grace preaching drops Paul's unless ye have believed in vain entirely, treating a past decision as sufficient regardless of whether faith perseveres.
corruption_paragraphs: A gospel presentation that ends at the moment of decision, with no accounting for perseverance, quietly removes 1 Corinthians 15:2's own conditional clause. Paul does not treat the initial believing as automatically self-sustaining; he ties final salvation to a faith that continues, unless it was believed in vain.

The Reformed answer is not doubt about assurance but the doctrine of perseverance itself: the elect are kept by God's power through faith, and that kept faith is precisely what answers Paul's unless. The warning drives the saint to Christ daily, not to anxious self-inspection alone.
roots_summary: Behind Paul's unless stands the Greek ektos ei me (ἔκτος εἰ μή), unless indeed, a strong conditional exception clause.
roots_lines: Unless in Leviticus governs ritual, not merely moral, cleanness.
Unless in Psalm 27 marks the single support of David's sanity.
Unless in Psalm 94 names the LORD outright as that support.
Unless in 1 Corinthians ties final salvation to a persevering faith.
In every instance the word narrows attention to one non-negotiable condition.
usage: Unless he wash his flesh with water — no partial obedience under the ceremonial law.
Unless I had believed to see the goodness of the LORD — faith as the thread of sanity.
Unless ye have believed in vain — Paul's warning against a faith that does not endure.

etymology: Old French aise, ease, comfort — comparative degree, less difficult, requiring less effort or cost.
biblical_def:
So shall it be easier for thyself. Whether is easier, to say, Thy sins be forgiven thee; or to say, Arise, and walk? It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God.

Scripture's easier is almost always a trap for false confidence. Jethro's counsel to Moses is the one plain, practical use: delegated judges will make the burden easier for thyself. Every other instance belongs to Christ, and each is a rhetorical question meant to expose what looks easy as actually impossible apart from divine power. It is far easier to speak forgiveness than to command a paralytic to walk — unless both are equally the prerogative of God alone, which is exactly Christ's point in healing the body to prove His authority over the soul. And it is easier for a camel to pass a needle's eye than for a rich man, trusting his riches, to enter the kingdom — a comparison built to be impossible by human effort, so that the disciples' next question, who then can be saved?, receives the only right answer: with God all things are possible.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from EASY: not difficult; requiring little labor or effort; comparative degree.
webster_full: EASY, a. That may be done, effected, or performed without difficulty.
Free from pain, anxiety, or distress; quiet; tranquil.
Complying; yielding; not obstinate.
EASIER, a. Comparative of Easy; less difficult, less burdensome.
Used by Christ in rhetorical comparisons that expose the impossibility of salvation by human effort or merit.
scriptures: And let them judge the people at all seasons: and it shall be, that every great matter they shall bring unto thee, but every small matter they shall judge: so shall it be easier for thyself, and they shall bear the burden with thee.
Mat 9:5
For whether is easier, to say, Thy sins be forgiven thee; or to say, Arise, and walk?
And again I say unto you, It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God.
And it is easier for heaven and earth to pass, than one tittle of the law to fail.
corruption_summary: Prosperity teaching reverses Matthew 19:24 into its opposite, treating wealth as evidence of divine favor that makes entrance into the kingdom easier rather than harder.
corruption_paragraphs: Where Christ names riches a near-impossible obstacle to entering the kingdom, prosperity theology names riches a sign that the kingdom has already been entered. The camel-and-needle saying is either softened into hyperbole or quietly dropped from the preaching rotation.

The text will not be softened: with men this is impossible, but with God all things are possible. The hardness is real and is meant to drive the rich, like every sinner, off self-reliance and onto sovereign grace, not to be explained away as rhetorical exaggeration.
roots_summary: Christ's easier in Matt. 19:24 renders the Greek eukopoteron (εὐκοπώτερον), of less toil, the same comparative He uses of forgiving sin versus commanding the lame to walk.
roots_lines: Easier in Exodus is Jethro's plain administrative wisdom.
Easier in Matthew 9 is a rhetorical trap exposing Christ's divine authority.
Easier in Matthew 19 makes wealth an obstacle, not an advantage, to the kingdom.
Luke 16:17 uses the same comparative to make Scripture's permanence, not its ease, the point.
Christ's rhetorical uses of easier all conclude with God, not man, as the one who makes the impossible possible.
usage: So shall it be easier for thyself — Jethro's counsel toward shared, sustainable burden.
Whether is easier, to forgive sins or to heal — Christ's proof of divine authority.
Easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle — wealth as obstacle, not merit.

etymology: Anglo-Saxon faeger, beautiful, pleasing to the eye — comparative degree, surpassing in beauty or appearance.
biblical_def:
Is not her younger sister fairer than she? Thou art fairer than the children of men: grace is poured into thy lips. Their countenances appeared fairer and fatter in flesh than all the children which did eat the portion of the king's meat.

Scripture uses fairer for ordinary beauty and then, in one verse, breaks the category open entirely. Samson's father-in-law offers a fairer sister as a worldly bargain, beauty as tradeable property, and the offer only deepens the tragedy already underway. Daniel's fairer is a providential sign hidden inside a dietary test: four young men who refuse the king's rich food are found, ten days later, fairer and fatter in flesh than their pampered peers, God honoring quiet obedience with visible health. But Psalm 45:2 lifts fairer past every merely human comparison: thou art fairer than the children of men, sung of the Messianic King, His surpassing beauty inseparable from the grace poured into His lips. No comparative in Scripture carries greater weight.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from FAIR: beautiful, handsome, pleasing to the eye; comparative degree, surpassing in beauty.
webster_full: FAIR, a. Beautiful; handsome; pleasing to the eye.
Clear; free from clouds or storms, as fair weather.
Free from blemish, imperfection, or impurity.
FAIRER, a. Comparative of Fair; surpassing in beauty, clearness, or favor.
Applied supremely in Scripture to Christ, whose fairness of person is inseparable from the grace of His speech.
scriptures: Jdg 15:2
And her father said, I verily thought that thou hadst utterly hated her; therefore I gave her to thy companion: is not her younger sister fairer than she? take her, I pray thee, instead of her.
Psa 45:2
Thou art fairer than the children of men: grace is poured into thy lips: therefore God hath blessed thee for ever.
Dan 1:15
And at the end of ten days their countenances appeared fairer and fatter in flesh than all the children which did eat the portion of the king's meat.
corruption_summary: Modern devotional reading of Psalm 45:2 often flattens it into generic praise poetry, missing that the Reformed and historic Christian reading takes the psalm as directly Messianic, applied to Christ Himself in Hebrews 1:8-9.
corruption_paragraphs: Treating Psalm 45 as merely a royal wedding song for an ancient Israelite king, with no further reference, strips the psalm of the very reading the New Testament itself supplies. Hebrews 1:8-9 quotes Psalm 45:6-7 directly of the Son, settling the psalm's ultimate referent beyond dispute.

This entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition beyond the point above. The principle to recover is that Old Testament royal psalms regularly reach past their immediate king to the true King, and fairer than the children of men is Scripture's own verdict on Christ, not a devotional embellishment added later.
roots_summary: Psalm 45:2's fairer renders yaphyapita (Heb.), an intensified doubling of yapheh, beautiful — fair beyond fairness itself.
roots_lines: Fairer in Judges is beauty offered as a bargaining chip, not a blessing.
Fairer in Daniel is providence rewarding covenant faithfulness in small things.
Fairer in Psalm 45 is intensified in the Hebrew beyond ordinary comparison.
The New Testament in Hebrews 1 applies the psalm's fairer directly to the Son.
No comparative adjective in the Psalter carries higher Christological freight.
usage: Is not her younger sister fairer than she? — beauty offered as worldly barter.
Fairer and fatter in flesh — providence rewarding Daniel's quiet obedience.
Thou art fairer than the children of men — the Messianic King's surpassing beauty.

etymology: Anglo-Saxon stif, rigid, inflexible — unyielding, resistant to bending, applied figuratively to obstinate resistance.
biblical_def:
Thy stiff neck. Speak not with a stiff neck. They made their neck stiff, that they might not hear, nor receive instruction.

Stiff neck is one of Scripture's most persistent figures for covenant rebellion, drawn from the image of an ox refusing the yoke, its neck rigid against the plow. Moses names Israel's stiff neck to their face at the very end of his life, the diagnosis he has repeated since Exodus 32. The Psalter turns the figure outward as counsel: do not speak with a stiff neck, do not let arrogance harden the very posture of the body into visible pride. Jeremiah completes the picture by making the stiffening a deliberate act — they made their neck stiff, that they might not hear — rebellion is not merely inherited weakness but chosen resistance to correction. Stephen's speech in Acts 7 will later gather the whole figure into one indictment: ye stiffnecked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, ye do always resist the Holy Ghost.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): not flexible; rigid; not easily bent; figuratively, obstinate, stubborn, unyielding to reason or authority.
webster_full: STIFF, a. Not easily bent; rigid; not pliant or flexible.
Not liquid or fluid; thick; inspissated.
Strong; violent; as, a stiff gale.
Obstinate; stubborn; pertinacious.
STIFF-NECKED, a. Stubborn; inflexible; obstinate; contumacious, as applied to Israel's covenant rebellion.
scriptures: For I know thy rebellion, and thy stiff neck: behold, while I am yet alive with you this day, ye have been rebellious against the LORD; and how much more after my death?
Psa 75:5
Lift not up your horn on high: speak not with a stiff neck.
But they obeyed not, neither inclined their ear, but made their neck stiff, that they might not hear, nor receive instruction.
corruption_summary: Modern therapeutic language recasts stubborn resistance to God's word as a personality trait or coping mechanism, dissolving the moral category the KJV names plainly as sin.
corruption_paragraphs: To call someone strong-willed or independent-minded where the text says stiff-necked quietly removes the covenant charge of rebellion and replaces it with a neutral or even admirable trait. Jeremiah is explicit that the stiffening is a refusal to hear and receive instruction, a moral act, not a temperament.

The remedy Scripture offers is not self-acceptance but a new heart: I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh (Ezek. 36:26). The stiff neck is bent only by sovereign grace, not by reframing the diagnosis.
roots_summary: The Hebrew idiom behind stiff neck is qesheh oreph, hard of neck, the image of a beast of burden resisting the yoke rather than submitting to its master's direction.
roots_lines: Stiff neck in Deuteronomy is Moses' final, unsoftened diagnosis of Israel.
Stiff neck in the Psalms is arrogance made visible in bodily posture.
Stiff neck in Jeremiah is a chosen refusal to hear correction.
Stephen's speech in Acts 7 gathers the figure into a single indictment of resisting the Holy Ghost.
The remedy is a new heart of flesh, not a reframed diagnosis.
usage: Thy rebellion, and thy stiff neck — Moses' final charge against Israel.
Speak not with a stiff neck — the Psalter's warning against visible arrogance.
They made their neck stiff, that they might not hear — rebellion as a chosen act.

etymology: Anglo-Saxon heard, firm, solid, difficult — comparative degree, more difficult, more resistant, more severe.
biblical_def:
A brother offended is harder to be won than a strong city. They have made their faces harder than a rock. As an adamant harder than flint have I made thy forehead.

Harder measures resistance, and Scripture uses it both to describe fallen obstinacy and to describe the prophetic toughness God supplies to meet it. Proverbs names relational rupture in blunt military terms: a brother offended is harder to be won than a strong city, and their contentions like the bars of a castle — wounded love fortifies itself against reconciliation. Jeremiah diagnoses the same hardness nationally: Judah has made their faces harder than a rock, refusing to blush at sin they no longer even feel as sin. Ezekiel's harder is different in kind: the LORD Himself makes the prophet's forehead as an adamant harder than flint, not to harden Ezekiel's heart but to arm him against a rebellious house that will not intimidate him into silence.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from HARD: firm; solid; not easily penetrated; difficult; comparative degree, more difficult or more obstinate.
webster_full: HARD, a. Firm; solid; compact; not easily penetrated, dented, or separated into parts.
Difficult; not easy to be done or accomplished.
Difficult to bear or endure; severe; distressing.
HARDER, a. Comparative of Hard; more difficult, more obstinate, more severe.
Applied to hardened conscience (Jeremiah) and to prophetic boldness given by God (Ezekiel) alike.
scriptures: A brother offended is harder to be won than a strong city: and their contentions are like the bars of a castle.
Jer 5:3

O LORD, are not thine eyes upon the truth? thou hast stricken them, but they have not grieved; thou hast consumed them, but they have refused to receive correction: they have made their faces harder than a rock; they have refused to return.
Eze 3:9
As an adamant harder than flint have I made thy forehead: fear them not, neither be dismayed at their looks, though they be a rebellious house.
corruption_summary: Conflict-avoidance culture treats Proverbs 18:19 as counsel to avoid ever giving offense, when the text is describing a fallen condition to be overcome by pursuit, not a warning to tiptoe around others' feelings indefinitely.
corruption_paragraphs: Read therapeutically, the offended brother becomes someone whose boundaries must never be tested, and reconciliation becomes optional. The proverb instead names how hard reconciliation actually is as a spur to pursue it earnestly, per Christ's own command in Matthew 18, not a reason to abandon the attempt.

Beyond the point above, this entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Christ's: if thy brother trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault, undeterred by how hard the walls have grown.
roots_summary: Ezekiel 3:9's harder than flint renders chizzaqah mitstsor (Heb.), a repeated intensive of hardness, the same root used of Pharaoh's hardened heart, here given by God for a righteous purpose.
roots_lines: Harder in Proverbs describes wounded relationship, not physical strength.
Harder in Jeremiah describes a conscience past the point of grief over sin.
Harder in Ezekiel is prophetic boldness supplied by God, not sinful obstinacy.
The same Hebrew root for hardness can describe both Pharaoh's rebellion and Ezekiel's God-given courage.
Context, not the word alone, determines whether harder names sin or strength.
usage: A brother offended is harder to be won than a strong city — the cost of ruptured relationship.
They have made their faces harder than a rock — a conscience past feeling grief over sin.
As an adamant harder than flint — God's gift of boldness to a prophet facing rebellion.

etymology: Anglo-Saxon-derived via Old Norse geta, to obtain, acquire — came into possession of, by labor, gift, or providence.
biblical_def:
All his substance, which he had got in the land of Canaan. I got me servants and maidens, and had servants born in my house. So I got a girdle according to the word of the LORD.

Got is Scripture's plain word for acquisition, and its object always reveals the character of the getting. Esau's substance was got in Canaan through ordinary increase, the narrator's bookkeeping before the family's final parting from Jacob. The Preacher's got in Ecclesiastes 2 is the record of a man testing whether accumulation itself can satisfy — servants, cattle, silver, gold, all got and found, in the end, vanity and vexation of spirit. Jeremiah's got is different in kind entirely: I got a girdle according to the word of the LORD, obedience to a strange prophetic sign-act rather than ordinary acquisition, the girdle's later ruin at the Euphrates becoming a living parable of Judah's own corruption.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from GET: obtained; acquired; gained possession of, by purchase, labor, or providence.
webster_full: GET, v.t. To obtain; to procure; to gain possession of by almost any means.
To beget, as offspring.
To learn; to commit to memory.
GOT, pp. Obtained; acquired; gained.
Used of ordinary increase (Genesis), tested accumulation (Ecclesiastes), and prophetic obedience (Jeremiah) alike.
scriptures: Gen 36:6

And Esau took his wives, and his sons, and his daughters, and all the persons of his house, and his cattle, and all his beasts, and all his substance, which he had got in the land of Canaan; and went into the country from the face of his brother Jacob.
Ecc 2:7
I got me servants and maidens, and had servants born in my house; also I had great possessions of great and small cattle above all that were in Jerusalem before me:
Jer 13:2
So I got a girdle according to the word of the LORD, and put it on my loins.
Jer 13:4
Take the girdle that thou hast got, which is upon thy loins, and arise, go to Euphrates, and hide it there in a hole of the rock.
corruption_summary: The prosperity gospel reads Ecclesiastes 2's catalog of everything got as a model for faithful accumulation, skipping past the Preacher's own verdict that it was all vanity and vexation of spirit.
corruption_paragraphs: Lifted out of context, I got me servants and maidens sounds like a testimony of blessing. Read to the end of the chapter, it is the opposite: the Preacher's experiment in getting everything under the sun concludes that none of it profits a man for all his labour which he taketh under the sun.

The corrective is Ecclesiastes' own conclusion: to eat, drink, and find enjoyment in one's labor is itself from the hand of God, not the accumulation that surrounds it. What is got means nothing without the Giver behind the getting.
roots_summary: Jeremiah's got renders qanah (Heb.), to acquire or procure, the same root behind the doctrine of God as Possessor and Redeemer who has procured a people for Himself.
roots_lines: Got in Genesis records ordinary providence in Esau's increase.
Got in Ecclesiastes catalogs a deliberate test of accumulation's power to satisfy.
Got in Jeremiah names obedience to a prophetic sign-act, not acquisition for gain.
The Hebrew qanah behind Jeremiah's got also underlies the doctrine of God's redeeming possession of His people.
What is got reveals its worth only in light of who gave it and why.
usage: All his substance, which he had got in the land of Canaan — ordinary providence and increase.
I got me servants and maidens — the Preacher's tested accumulation, found vanity.
So I got a girdle according to the word of the LORD — obedience to a prophetic sign.

pos: verb (archaic 3rd person singular present of use)
etymology: Old French user, to employ, from Latin uti, to use — archaic third-person singular ending -eth in place of modern -s.
biblical_def:
That useth divination. The tongue of the wise useth knowledge aright. Every one that useth milk is unskilful in the word of righteousness.

Useth marks habitual practice, the settled pattern of a life rather than a single act. Moses lists the man that useth divination among the forbidden occult practices of the nations Israel is displacing, a habit of consulting powers other than the LORD. Proverbs turns the same verb toward speech: the tongue of the wise useth knowledge aright, wisdom shown not in possessing knowledge but in habitually deploying it rightly, while the poor useth intreaties and the rich answereth roughly, exposing how wealth coarsens a man's habitual speech. The writer to the Hebrews completes the pattern spiritually: every one that useth milk is unskilful in the word of righteousness, an infant diet becoming, if never outgrown, the mark of a believer who has not habitually exercised his senses to discern good and evil.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from USE: to employ for a purpose; to practice customarily or habitually; archaic third-person form.
webster_full: USE, v.t. To employ; to apply to one's service; to make use of.
To practice customarily; to accustom; to habituate.
USETH, v. Archaic third-person singular of Use; customarily employs or practices.
Applied to habitual occult practice (Deuteronomy), habitual right or coarse speech (Proverbs), and habitual spiritual immaturity (Hebrews).
The -eth ending, standard in the Authorized Version, was already archaic by 1611 in ordinary speech but retained for solemnity and precision.
scriptures: There shall not be found among you any one that maketh his son or his daughter to pass through the fire, or that useth divination, or an observer of times, or an enchanter, or a witch,
Pro 15:2
The tongue of the wise useth knowledge aright: but the mouth of fools poureth out foolishness.
The poor useth intreaties; but the rich answereth roughly.
Heb 5:13
For every one that useth milk is unskilful in the word of righteousness: for he is a babe.
corruption_summary: Modern occult practices (astrology apps, tarot, mediums marketed as wellness) are repackaged as harmless self-discovery, obscuring that Deuteronomy 18 names habitual divination an abomination the LORD drove nations out for practicing.
corruption_paragraphs: Horoscopes and psychic consultation are widely treated as light entertainment or personal empowerment rather than what Deuteronomy 18:10-12 calls it: an abomination unto the LORD, grouped with child sacrifice as the reason the Canaanite nations were dispossessed.

The corrective is not superstition about the practices themselves but the positive alternative Deuteronomy 18 immediately supplies: the LORD thy God will raise up unto thee a Prophet, ultimately fulfilled in Christ, the sole and sufficient mediator of God's will, who displaces every substitute source of guidance.
roots_summary: Hebrews 5:13's useth milk renders metechon (μετέχων), partaking of, paired with nepios, infant — the whole phrase naming arrested spiritual growth.
roots_lines: Useth in Deuteronomy names habitual occult practice, not a single lapse.
Useth in Proverbs 15 names the wise man's habitual right use of knowledge in speech.
Useth in Proverbs 18 exposes how wealth habitually coarsens a man's speech.
Useth in Hebrews names habitual spiritual infancy, milk never exchanged for meat.
The archaic -eth ending was already old-fashioned in 1611, retained by the translators for solemn precision.
usage: That useth divination — forbidden occult practice among the nations Israel displaced.
The tongue of the wise useth knowledge aright — wisdom as habitual right speech.
Every one that useth milk is unskilful in the word of righteousness — arrested spiritual growth.

etymology: Anglo-Saxon self, same, own person — plural reflexive form intensifying the identity of the subject.
biblical_def:
Ye see and know of your own selves that summer is now nigh at hand. Also of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things. First gave their own selves to the Lord. Deceiving your own selves.

Own selves is Scripture's phrase for unmediated, personal knowledge and responsibility, most often used to strip away every excuse of ignorance. Christ tells the disciples they know of their own selves, without needing a further sign, that summer is near — the same immediate perception should read the signs of the times. Paul warns the Ephesian elders that of your own selves shall men arise, apostasy's most dangerous source being internal, not external. The Corinthians' gift of themselves models the opposite: they first gave their own selves to the Lord before giving anything else. James closes the pattern with a warning: hearers who are not doers are deceiving their own selves, self-deception being uniquely inexcusable because it is self-inflicted.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from SELF: plural form; one's own person, used reflexively or emphatically to denote personal, unmediated agency.
webster_full: SELF, pron. The same; used to express identity, or particular person.
In compounds, expressing that an action is performed by the same person that receives its effect.
SELVES, pron. Plural of Self; used reflexively for emphasis on personal responsibility.
Own selves in Scripture strips away appeal to ignorance or external excuse.
Used both of right perception (Luke), internal apostasy (Acts), self-giving (2 Corinthians), and self-deception (James).
scriptures: When they now shoot forth, ye see and know of your own selves that summer is now nigh at hand.
Also of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them.
And this they did, not as we hoped, but first gave their own selves to the Lord, and unto us by the will of God.
Jas 1:22
But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.
corruption_summary: Modern individualism reads own selves through a therapeutic lens of authenticity and self-actualization, missing that every biblical use ties selves to accountability before God, not autonomy from Him.
corruption_paragraphs: Be true to yourself culture treats selves as the final court of appeal. Scripture's own selves is never autonomous; in Acts 20:30 it names the very danger of unaccountable internal corruption, and in James 1:22 self-deception is the specific charge against those who trust their own hearing without doing.

The remedy is 2 Corinthians 8:5's pattern: the Macedonians first gave their own selves to the Lord, and only then to the apostolic mission. Selves rightly ordered are selves surrendered, not selves asserted.
roots_summary: Acts 20:30's own selves renders ex hymon auton (ἐξ ὑμ᳦ν αὐτῶν), from among yourselves, Paul's warning that apostasy's most dangerous source is internal to the church.
roots_lines: Own selves in Luke names unmediated, inexcusable perception.
Own selves in Acts names the internal source of coming apostasy.
Own selves in 2 Corinthians models self-giving that precedes all other giving.
Own selves in James names self-deception as uniquely without excuse.
In every case, selves are accountable before God, never autonomous from Him.
usage: Ye see and know of your own selves — unmediated, inexcusable spiritual perception.
Of your own selves shall men arise — the internal danger of coming apostasy.
Deceiving your own selves — James's charge against hearers who are not doers.

etymology: Anglo-Saxon lang, extended in space or time — comparative degree, of greater duration or extent.
biblical_def:
She could not longer hide him. They could not any longer stand before their enemies. What should I wait for the LORD any longer? The LORD could no longer bear.

No longer marks the breaking point where endurance gives way, and Scripture uses it at some of its most decisive turns. Jochebed's could not longer hide him is the hinge of the whole exodus narrative: the moment concealment fails is the moment Moses is set adrift, and providence, not the mother's ingenuity, carries him from there. Israel's could not any longer stand before their enemies names covenant unfaithfulness reaching its consequence under the judges. The unnamed king's any longer in 2 Kings voices the despair of a starving, besieged Samaria giving up on the LORD's deliverance almost at the moment it arrives. And Jeremiah's could no longer bear is spoken of God Himself, patience exhausted by persistent, unrepented sin, immediately followed by the desolation Judah has stored up.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from LONG: of great extent in space or duration; comparative degree, of greater duration.
webster_full: LONG, a. Extended in space, or in time; not short.
Continued or protracted; as, a long debate.
LONGER, a. Comparative of Long; of greater duration or extent.
No longer: a phrase marking the cessation of a preceding state or the exhaustion of endurance.
Applied in Scripture to human concealment failing (Exodus), covenant strength failing (Judges), human patience failing (2 Kings), and divine patience reaching its limit (Jeremiah).
scriptures: Exo 2:3
And when she could not longer hide him, she took for him an ark of bulrushes, and daubed it with slime and with pitch, and put the child therein; and she laid it in the flags by the river's brink.
Jdg 2:14

And the anger of the LORD was hot against Israel, and he delivered them into the hands of spoilers that spoiled them, and he sold them into the hands of their enemies round about, so that they could not any longer stand before their enemies.
And while he yet talked with them, behold, the messenger came down unto him: and he said, Behold, this evil is of the LORD; what should I wait for the LORD any longer?

So that the LORD could no longer bear, because of the evil of your doings, and because of the abominations which ye have committed; therefore is your land a desolation, and an astonishment, and a curse, without an inhabitant, as at this day.
corruption_summary: A therapeutic reading of divine patience treats God's could no longer bear as an anthropomorphic embarrassment to be explained away, when Jeremiah presents it as the sober conclusion of real, righteous judgment.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern discomfort with divine wrath sometimes recasts the LORD could no longer bear as primitive or merely figurative, distancing the text from a God who actually judges sin. Jeremiah offers the phrase as the hinge of an entire historical argument: the desolation of the land is because of, not despite, the LORD's righteous exhaustion of patience with persistent evil.

The corrective is to hold divine patience and divine justice together as Scripture does: the LORD is longsuffering, not willing that any should perish, yet His patience has a real limit reached by real, unrepented sin, and that limit is itself an act of justice, not a loss of temper.
roots_summary: Jeremiah's could no longer bear renders lo yakol se'th (Heb.), was not able to bear or carry, the same verb used of a burden too heavy to lift.
roots_lines: Longer in Exodus marks the failure of human concealment at the hinge of the exodus story.
Longer in Judges marks covenant unfaithfulness reaching its military consequence.
Longer in 2 Kings voices human despair on the very edge of deliverance.
Longer in Jeremiah is spoken of God's own patience reaching its righteous limit.
The Hebrew behind Jeremiah's phrase pictures a burden no longer able to be carried.
usage: She could not longer hide him — the hinge moment of the exodus narrative.
They could not any longer stand before their enemies — covenant unfaithfulness under the judges.
The LORD could no longer bear — divine patience reaching its righteous limit in Jeremiah.
